title: What the homepage has to prove for a consumer brand
metaTitle: What a brand homepage has to prove
excerpt: A brand homepage should show the object clearly and offer a way to see the product. A manifesto before the product leaves a new shopper with nothing to judge.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf. Objects you can name, which is what a brand homepage has to lead with.
caption: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase on a white shelf. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a brand homepage show?
faqs.answer: Show the object large enough to name, one plain sentence about what it is, and a single way to see the product. A second family of goods can sit smaller, if it prevents a wrong conclusion. A manifesto can wait until the thing is identified.

faqs.question: Where should the brand story go?
faqs.answer: Put one or two sentences on material or method after the object, if those facts change the purchase. The longer story belongs on the about page for someone who is already interested. Leading with belief asks a stranger to agree before they know what you sell.

faqs.question: How do you test the first screen?
faqs.answer: Cover the logo and ask someone who has never bought from you to name the object and point to it. If they describe a feeling and cannot find the product, the screen is still a mood. Repeat the test on a phone, outdoors.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A consumer brand homepage has one job for a shopper who does not know you yet. Show the object clearly, and offer a way to see the product. A manifesto before the product fails that shopper. They cannot join a belief they have not seen attached to a thing they might buy.

The first screen is a counter. What is this. Is it for me. How do I look closer. Answer those, in that order, before you explain the company.

## The object, at a size a stranger can name

Put the product in the first view, photographed so the shape, the material, and the use are legible. A mug should look like a mug that fits a hand. A jacket should show the cut, not only a texture of cloth. A tool should show the working end. If the shopper cannot say what they are looking at, the brand has not started.

Lifestyle can support the object. It should not replace it. A room where the product is a blur in the background is a mood. The shopper came to find out what you sell. Mood is a second glance, after the thing is identified. Crop with that sequence in mind. Object first, context second, atmosphere last.

Wabisabi is a public Hanabi project: a calm brand site. The lesson to take is restraint around the object, a visual quiet that lets the thing be seen. It is not a template, and it is not a claim about sales. Down the Cove is the public ecommerce example: a restructure, migration, and redesign of a shop, including the move off an older stack. The homepage lesson from that kind of work is the same. The catalog has to be recognizable as objects, with a point of view in how they are shown.

Nielsen Norman Group's article on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the time box. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds. Value has to be clear within about 10 seconds if you want longer attention, and people read only about a quarter of the text. A manifesto spends the quarter on the maker's feelings. The object spends it on the decision.

## A way to see the product

Beside or beneath the object, give one action in the shopper's words. Shop the mug. See the jacket. View the set. The destination should be the product, or a tight collection of the thing the picture showed. A button that says Explore, or Discover the world, opens a hallway.

If you sell more than one kind of thing, the first screen can show the primary object and a short row of the other families, each with its own picture and its own name. Three families is a choice. Twelve families is a stockroom. Edit until a new shopper can point at one.

The price can appear on the homepage when it changes the decision and you can keep it true. A single hero product with a price is honest. A homepage that implies a price you do not honor on the product page is a quarrel inside the brand. When prices vary, skip the number on the homepage and make the path to the product short enough that the number is the next fact they see.

Name the product in ordinary words. The poetic name can sit beside a plain description. "Coast mug, a 300 ml cup that fits under a standard machine." The plain half is what a stranger repeats to themselves. The poetic half is the brand. You need both, and the plain half has to come early enough to be read.

## Where the manifesto waits

The story of why you make the thing can be true and still be early. A shopper who has not identified the object cannot use your values. Place the short version after the object and the path: one or two sentences on material, place, or method, if those facts change why this object exists. The long version belongs on the about page, for the person who is already interested.

"We believe in slower mornings" above a photograph of mist is a manifesto. "A stoneware mug, made in small batches, shown here at actual scale" is an offer. You can believe in slower mornings and still lead with the mug. The belief becomes credible when the object supports it. In the other order, the belief is a demand that the shopper agree before they are allowed to see the goods.

Founders often defend the manifesto because it is the part they enjoyed writing. The shopper is not in that meeting. Read the first screen with the company name covered. If it could belong to any careful brand, the screen is still a mood. Put the distinctive object back until the screen could only be you.

Campaign lines can rotate only if each line still points at a product you have. A seasonal sentence with a link to that season's object is a campaign. A rotating set of abstract claims is a manifesto in costume. When the season ends, remove the line. A homepage that still announces last winter's drop tells the shopper you are not watching the store.

## The first screen, written as a list

Hold the first view to a few parts.

- One photograph of the object, clear enough to name.
- The name, and one plain sentence on what it is.
- A single way to see the product.
- An optional second object or collection, visibly secondary.

Everything else can scroll. Materials in more detail. A note on shipping. A short maker line. Reviews, if they are real and specific. The journal, if you truly keep one. Put the journal last. A shopper who wants an essay will scroll. A shopper who wants the thing should not have to.

Type should sound like a person who has held the product. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. Avoid a headline that only works if you already love the brand. You are speaking to someone who does not know you yet. Clarity is the courtesy.

On a phone, stack picture, sentence, and link. Do not let a wide editorial layout decide the order. The object can be large. The link has to share the first view. A beautiful crop with the button stranded below is a poster, and posters do not sell a second look so much as they ask for patience the research says you may not get.

## What the rest of the homepage is for

After the first view, show a small set of products with the same photographic rules. Consistent ground, consistent crop, price if the price is simple. The set should feel chosen. A brand shop is an edited room. It is a poor impersonation of a marketplace grid with infinite tiles and no point of view.

Then one proof that a person stands behind the goods. A maker's hands, a material, a place, in a single band with a sentence and a link to the about page. Then a practical band: shipping region, returns in one line, and a link to the policy. Practical facts reduce the risk of looking closer. They are part of showing the product, because "see the product" includes believing the shop is real.

Skip a popup that covers the object to offer a discount code. If you use a code, put it in a banner that does not hide the thing. The object is the reason to stay. Covering it for an email address reverses the priority. You can ask for the address after a product view, or in the footer, where it does not tax the first 10 seconds.

Hanabi's public shop work, including Down the Cove's migration and redesign, treats the homepage as the start of a catalog with a point of view. The studio designs and builds. The brand still has to know which object leads. No layout can choose that for you.

Check the first screen with the logo covered and the brand name hidden. Ask a person who has never bought from you to say what the object is and where they would tap to see it. If they describe a feeling and cannot find the product, the manifesto is still in the way. If they name the object and point at the link, the homepage is doing the job. Repeat the test on a phone, outdoors, because that is the visit you will actually get.

A second object can appear, smaller, when it prevents a wrong conclusion. A brand that sells a bottle and a refill should not let the homepage imply that the bottle is the only thing, or that the refill includes the bottle. One secondary frame, labeled, is enough. A carousel of six moods is how the test starts failing again.

## Then they will ask what it costs to say yes

Once the object is clear, a careful shopper looks for the price and for what the price includes. Shipping, a refill, a set, a size. Hiding that shape forces a conversation you could have finished on the page. The next piece is [a pricing page for a consumer brand](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-consumer-brand).

If you want to talk through what the first screen should prove before you redesign, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the object you would put in a stranger's hand first.
